extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, federal agency IP managers, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Statutory standards from the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure and 35 U.S.C. governing licensing of government-owned inventions, reissue/disclaimer/correction procedures, supplemental examination, ownership/assignment, joint ownership, and infringement definitions and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of Commerce authority to promulgate licensing regulations (35 U.S.C. 208)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of Commerce is authorized to promulgate regulations specifying the terms and conditions upon which any federally owned invention, other than inventions owned by the Tennessee Valley Authority, may be licensed on a nonexclusive, partially exclusive, or exclusive basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grants regulatory authority to set licensing rules for federally owned inventions; applies broadly except TVA-owned inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive/partially exclusive license: incentive requirement (35 U.S.C. 209(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A Federal agency may grant an exclusive or partially exclusive license only if granting the license is a reasonable and necessary incentive to (A) call forth the investment capital and expenditures needed to bring the invention to practical application; or (B) otherwise promote the invention’s utilization by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must find exclusivity is justified by the need to attract investment or promote utilization; the showing relates to practical application or public utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive/partially exclusive license: public_served_and_scope_limit (35 U.S.C. 209(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal agency finds that the public will be served by the granting of the license, as indicated by the applicant’s intentions, plans, and ability to bring the invention to practical application or otherwise promote the invention’s utilization by the public, and that the proposed scope of exclusivity is not greater than reasonably necessary to provide the incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment based on applicant's stated intentions/plans/ability; scope of exclusivity must be no greater than necessary to provide the incentive claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to achieve practical application within reasonable time (35 U.S.C. 209(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant makes a commitment to achieve practical application of the invention within a reasonable time, which time may be extended by the agency upon the applicant’s request and the applicant’s demonstration that the refusal of such extension would be unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees must commit to development/marketing timelines; agencies can grant extensions upon justified request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust / competition safeguard for granting licenses (35 U.S.C. 209(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting the license will not tend to substantially lessen competition or create or maintain a violation of the Federal antitrust laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must consider antitrust impacts before granting exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent considerations for licensing (35 U.S.C. 209(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of an invention covered by a foreign patent application or patent, the interests of the Federal Government or United States industry in foreign commerce will be enhanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When foreign patents exist, agency should consider enhancement of U.S. government or industry interests in foreign commerce as a factor for exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture-in-the-United-States preference (35 U.S.C. 209(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A Federal agency shall normally grant a license to use or sell any federally owned invention in the United States only to a licensee who agrees that any products embodying the invention or produced through the use of the invention will be manufactured substantially in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard 'substantial manufacture in the U.S.' requirement applies normally to licensees for U.S. use/sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small business preference for exclusive licenses (35 U.S.C. 209(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: First preference for the granting of any exclusive or partially exclusive licenses shall be given to small business firms having equal or greater likelihood as other applicants to bring the invention to practical application within a reasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must give first preference to small businesses when they are as likely as others to commercialize the invention in reasonable time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required license terms and government retained license (35 U.S.C. 209(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any licenses shall contain such terms and conditions as the granting agency considers appropriate, and shall include provisions retaining a nontransferable, irrevocable, paid-up license for any Federal agency to practice the invention or have the invention practiced throughout the world by or on behalf of the Government of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must include a worldwide government-use reserved license in any granted license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic reporting requirement and confidentiality (35 U.S.C. 209(d)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses shall include provisions requiring periodic reporting on utilization of the invention, and utilization efforts, by the licensee, but only to the extent necessary to enable the Federal agency to determine whether the terms of the license are being complied with; such reports shall be treated as commercial and financial information privileged and confidential and not subject to disclosure under section 552 of title 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting scope limited to necessary information; reports are confidential and exempt from FOIA disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency termination power for nonperformance or breaches (35 U.S.C. 209(d)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses shall empower the Federal agency to terminate the license in whole or in part if the agency determines that: (A) the licensee is not executing its commitment to achieve practical application; (B) the licensee is in breach of a manufacture-in-U.S. agreement; (C) termination is necessary to meet requirements for public use specified by later regulations and such requirements are not reasonably satisfied by the licensee; or (D) the licensee has been found by a court of competent jurisdiction to have violated Federal antitrust laws in connection with its performance under the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termination grounds are explicit and include failure to commercialize, breach of domestic manufacture requirement, subsequent public-use regulatory requirements, and antitrust violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice and comment before granting exclusive license (35 U.S.C. 209(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: No exclusive or partially exclusive license may be granted unless public notice of the intention to grant has been provided in an appropriate manner at least 15 days before the license is granted, and the Federal agency has considered all comments received before the end of the comment period; exception for inventions made under a cooperative research and development agreement under 15 U.S.C. 3710a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must publish notice and consider comments at least 15 days prior to granting exclusivity, subject to statutory exception for CRADAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for development or marketing required (35 U.S.C. 209(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: No Federal agency shall grant any license under a patent or patent application on a federally owned invention unless the person requesting the license has supplied the agency with a plan for development or marketing of the invention; any such plan shall be treated as commercial and financial confidential information not subject to disclosure under section 552 of title 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must submit a development/marketing plan; plan is confidential and exempt from FOIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue of defective patents: grounds and prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C. 251)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any patent is, through error, deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim, the Director shall, on surrender of the patent and payment of the fee, reissue the patent for the invention disclosed in the original patent; no new matter shall be introduced into the application for reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue corrects defects in specification/drawings or incorrect claim scope; reissue cannot add new matter beyond original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple reissued patents allowed (35 U.S.C. 251(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may issue several reissued patents for distinct and separate parts of the thing patented, upon demand of the applicant, and upon payment of the required fee for a reissue for each such reissued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may request multiple reissues dividing the original patent into parts, subject to fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on enlarging claim scope in reissue (35 U.S.C. 251(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: No reissued patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To broaden claim scope via reissue, application must be filed within two years of original grant (statutory time limit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer and dedication requirements (35 U.S.C. 253)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may, on payment of the required fee, make disclaimer of any complete claim, stating the extent of his interest; such disclaimer shall be in writing and recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office and shall thereafter be considered as part of the original patent; likewise a patentee may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire term or any terminal part of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers must be written, recorded, and are effective as part of the patent; dedication of term possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reissue on prior actions and prior users (35 U.S.C. 252)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender of the original patent takes effect upon issue of the reissued patent; every reissued patent has same legal effect as if originally granted in amended form. Reissue shall not abridge or affect the right of any person who, prior to the grant of a reissue, made, purchased, offered to sell, used, or imported the patented thing to continue such activities unless doing so infringes a valid claim of the reissued patent that was in the original patent; courts may provide equitable terms protecting investments begun before reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue generally continues patent effect retroactively, but prior users are protected from being suddenly barred except to extent they would infringe valid original claims; courts have equitable powers to protect pre-existing investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of correction for PTO mistake (35 U.S.C. 254)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a mistake in a patent, incurred through the fault of the Patent and Trademark Office, is clearly disclosed by the records of the Office, the Director may issue a certificate of correction stating the fact and nature of such mistake, under seal, without charge, to be recorded in the records of patents. A printed copy shall be attached to each printed copy of the patent, and such certificate shall be considered as part of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO-correctable errors (its own fault) may be corrected without charge and the certificate becomes part of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of correction for applicant's mistake (35 U.S.C. 255)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a mistake of a clerical or typographical nature, or of minor character, which was not the fault of the Patent and Trademark Office, appears in a patent and a showing has been made that such mistake occurred in good faith, the Director may, upon payment of the required fee, issue a certificate of correction, if the correction does not involve such changes as would constitute new matter or require reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant errors of minor nature may be corrected upon fee and good-faith showing; corrections cannot introduce new matter or require reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of named inventor (35 U.S.C. 256)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever through error a person is named in an issued patent as the inventor, or through error an inventor is not named, the Director may, on application of all the parties and assignees, with proof of the facts and such other requirements as may be imposed, issue a certificate correcting such error. The error shall not invalidate the patent if it can be corrected as provided; courts may order correction on notice and hearing and the Director shall issue a certificate accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventorship errors may be corrected administratively by agreement and proof, or judicially on court order; correction preserves patent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination: request, timing, and certificate (35 U.S.C. 257(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may request supplemental examination of a patent to consider, reconsider, or correct information believed to be relevant to the patent, in accordance with requirements the Director may establish. Within 3 months after receipt of a compliant request, the Director shall conduct the supplemental examination and conclude by issuing a certificate indicating whether the information presented raises a substantial new question of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination is initiated by patent owner; Director must act within statutory 3-month window and issue a certificate stating whether a substantial new question (SNQ) exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination ordered if substantial new question raised (35 U.S.C. 257(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the certificate indicates that a substantial new question of patentability is raised by one or more items in the request, the Director shall order reexamination of the patent, conducted according to chapter 30 procedures, except the patent owner shall not have the right to file a statement pursuant to section 304. During reexamination, the Director shall address each substantial new question of patentability identified during the supplemental examination, notwithstanding limitations in chapter 30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental exam can trigger reexamination; Director must address each SNQ even if chapter 30 contains limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of supplemental examination on unenforceability defenses (35 U.S.C. 257(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall not be held unenforceable on the basis of conduct relating to information that had not been considered, was inadequately considered, or was incorrect in a prior examination of the patent if the information was considered, reconsidered, or corrected during a supplemental examination of the patent. The making of a request, or absence thereof, shall not be relevant to enforceability of the patent under section 282.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completing supplemental examination addressing previously unconsidered/misconsidered information can preclude certain unenforceability defenses (e.g., inequitable conduct) based on that information, subject to statutory exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to supplemental examination effect (35 U.S.C. 257(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (1) does not apply to (A) prior allegations pled with particularity in a civil action or set forth with particularity in certain statutory notices before the date of a supplemental examination request; and (B) in certain patent enforcement actions, defenses based upon information considered pursuant to a supplemental examination request unless the supplemental examination and any ordered reexamination are concluded before the date on which the action is brought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination does not immunize against allegations already pled with particularity prior to the request, nor against certain defenses in enforcement actions unless the processes conclude before litigation starts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and regulations for supplemental examination (35 U.S.C. 257(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall, by regulation, establish fees for submission of a request for supplemental examination and to consider each item of information submitted. If reexamination is ordered, fees applicable to ex parte reexamination shall be paid in addition to supplemental exam fees. The Director shall issue regulations governing form, content, and other requirements of requests and procedures for reviewing information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination is fee-based and subject to Director's implementing regulations on form/content and process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud referral during supplemental examination (35 U.S.C. 257(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Director becomes aware during supplemental examination or reexamination that a material fraud on the Office may have been committed in connection with the patent, the Director shall refer the matter to the Attorney General for further action; such referral shall be treated as confidential, not included in the patent file, and not disclosed unless the United States charges a person with a criminal offense in connection with the referral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential material fraud discovered in the process triggers confidential referral to DOJ; may result in criminal or other actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction for supplemental examination (35 U.S.C. 257(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in this section shall be construed to preclude imposition of sanctions based on criminal or antitrust laws, to limit the authority of the Director to investigate issues of possible misconduct and impose sanctions for misconduct before the Office, or to limit the Director's authority to issue regulations under chapter 3 relating to sanctions for misconduct by practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination provisions do not limit other enforcement or sanctioning authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and assignment: patents as personal property and PTO recording (35 U.S.C. 261)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to the provisions of this title, patents shall have the attributes of personal property. The Patent and Trademark Office shall maintain a register of interests in patents and applications and shall record any document related thereto upon request, and may require a fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents treated like personal property; PTO maintains official records of interests and records documents for fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments must be in writing and recording requirement (35 U.S.C. 261)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications for patent, patents, or any interest therein, shall be assignable in law by an instrument in writing. A certificate of acknowledgment of proper execution shall be prima facie evidence of execution. An assignment is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for valuable consideration without notice unless recorded in the PTO within three months from its date or prior to the date of such subsequent purchase or mortgage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments require writing; proper acknowledgment creates prima facie evidence; recording within statutory window protects against subsequent bona fide purchasers/mortgagees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint owners' rights in absence of agreement (35 U.S.C. 262)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of any agreement to the contrary, each of the joint owners of a patent may make, use, offer to sell, or sell the patented invention within the United States, or import the patented invention into the United States, without the consent of and without accounting to the other owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint ownership generally allows each owner independent exploitation rights unless a contrary agreement exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement defined (35 U.S.C. 271(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise provided in this title, whoever without authority makes, uses, offers to sell, or sells any patented invention within the United States, or imports into the United States any patented invention during the term of the patent therefor, infringes the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic statutory definition of acts that constitute direct infringement in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active inducement liability (35 U.S.C. 271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever actively induces infringement of a patent shall be liable as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inducement (encouraging others to infringe) creates direct liability separate from making/using/selling acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement criteria for components (35 U.S.C. 271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever offers to sell or sells within the United States or imports into the United States a component of a patented machine, manufacture, combination, or composition, or a material or apparatus for use in practicing a patented process, constituting a material part of the invention, knowing the same to be especially made or especially adapted for use in an infringement of such patent, and not a staple article or commodity of commerce suitable for substantial noninfringing use, shall be liable as a contributory infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability attaches where component is a material part, known to be specially made/adapted for infringing use, and not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted patentee conduct not amounting to misuse (35 U.S.C. 271(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent owner otherwise entitled to relief for infringement or contributory infringement shall be denied relief or deemed guilty of misuse or illegal extension of the patent right by reason of his having done one or more of the following: (1) derived revenue from acts which if performed by another without consent would constitute contributory infringement; (2) licensed or authorized another to perform acts which if performed without consent would constitute contributory infringement; (3) sought to enforce his patent rights against infringement or contributory infringement; (4) refused to license or use any rights to the patent; or (5) conditioned the license or sale on acquisition of another license or product, unless the patent owner has market power in the relevant market on which the license or sale is conditioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory list of patentee actions that do not, per se, constitute misuse, subject to market-power caveat for conditioning licenses/sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory submission safe harbor (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall not be an act of infringement to make, use, offer to sell, or sell within the United States or import into the United States a patented invention solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information under a Federal law which regulates the manufacture, use, or sale of drugs or veterinary biological products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a statutory experimental/use exception (regulatory submission safe harbor) for certain FDA-related development activities; limited to uses reasonably related to regulatory submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of certain drug applications may be act of infringement (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be an act of infringement to submit — (A) an application under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or described in section 505(b)(2) for a drug claimed in a patent or the use of which is claimed in a patent; (B) an application under section 512 or under the Act of March 4, 1913 for certain drugs or veterinary biological products claimed in a patent — (text truncated in source).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute addresses specific situations where submission of regulatory applications can implicate infringement; full statutory text should be consulted for scope and exceptions (source chunk truncates complete provision).
